  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

</span></span>

</span>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Generalizing metric monocular depth estimation presents a significant challenge due to its ill-posed nature, while the entanglement between camera parameters and depth amplifies issues further, hindering multi-dataset training and zero-shot accuracy.
This challenge is particularly evident in autonomous vehicles and mobile robotics, where data is collected with fixed camera setups, limiting the geometric diversity.
Yet, this context also presents an opportunity: the fixed relationship between the camera and the ground plane imposes additional perspective geometry constraints, enabling depth regression via vertical image positions of objects.
However, this cue is highly susceptible to overfitting, thus we propose a novel canonical representation that maintains consistency across varied camera setups, effectively disentangling depth from specific parameters and enhancing generalization across datasets.
We also propose a novel architecture that adaptively and probabilistically fuses depths estimated via object size and vertical image position cues.
A comprehensive evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach on five autonomous driving datasets, achieving accurate metric depth estimation for varying resolutions, aspect ratios and camera setups.
Notably, we achieve comparable accuracy to existing zero-shot methods, despite training on a single dataset with a single-camera setup. Project website: <a href="https://unizgfer-lamor.github.io/gvdepth/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_bold">https://unizgfer-lamor.github.io/gvdepth/</a></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Accurate 3D reconstruction is one of the fundamental computer vision challenges, with far-reaching applications across various fields.
Unlike multi-view approaches that rely on complex dense matching and pose estimation, learning-based Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) exploits semantic and geometric cues to infer pixel-wise depth maps from a single image.
However, <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">these cues are often specific to a narrow distribution of the training data</em>, resulting in poor generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2412.06080v2/intro.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/509;" width="685" height="509" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Proposed Vertical Canonical Representation.<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We introduce a novel intermediate representation that enables exploitation of underlying planar geometry priors, facilitating learning and generalization across varying camera setups. Under this representation, camera parameters and depth are completely disentangled, enabling depth regression via known depth of the ground plane.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the environmental domain gap, MDE is particularly sensitive to the domain gap induced by the perspective geometry parameters of the camera system.
This issue is present in most supervised <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> and self-supervised methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> that are trained on a dataset collected with a single camera system.
Models tend to overfit to this perspective geometry bias, leading to significant performance degradation when inferring depth with different cameras.
Unfortunately, training a MDE model on data with a wide distribution of perspective geometries is far from trivial.
Due to the inherent ambiguity of the MDE problem and entanglement of depth and camera parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, many methods resort to relative depth estimation with unknown shift and scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>.
Recently, zero-shot metric depth estimation has been achieved with various approaches, including embedding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, estimating <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> or disentangling the camera parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.
While these methods present impressive results, <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">they require large-scale training on data acquired from multiple camera systems</em>, which is not always practical or cost-effective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One specific area with numerous applications across varying fields is MDE for ground-based vehicles and robots.
In this context, an additional perspective geometry constraint arises due to the fixed position of the camera relative to the ground plane.
This constraint induces an additional depth cue: the vertical image position of the ground-contact point, which has been shown to be a dominant cue in autonomous driving scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These findings motivate us to utilize the vertical image position cue and the inherent planarity of the scene in order to enable accurate depth estimation and improve generalization for arbitrary intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters.
Contrary to the object size cue, widely used by the aforementioned zero-shot methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">we argue that the vertical image position presents a cue that is more fundamentally rooted in the perspective geometry configuration of the scene</em>.
However, without proper modeling, this cue is highly susceptible to overfitting to the specific camera system present in the training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To leverage this cue, while enabling training with diverse perspective geometries and zero-shot generalization, in this paper we propose a method to ensure its consistency for arbitrary camera setups.
Specifically, we introduce a novel intermediate depth representation termed <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vertical Canonical Representation</span>.
Rather than directly regressing depth values, our model predicts vertical image positions of the orthogonal projections of points onto the ground plane, as visualized in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
By utilizing the known depth of the ground plane, this approach allows the mapping between the canonical representation and depth space to adapt with varying camera parameters, effectively disentangling the vertical position cue from specific perspective geometry.
To further address potential errors in certain regions, we introduce an architecture that adaptively fuses depth predictions from both vertical position and object size cues, guided by dynamically estimated uncertainties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We comprehensively evaluate our method’s zero-shot capability on five autonomous driving datasets, analyzing its robustness and accuracy across various cues. We demonstrate that our approach matches the accuracy of existing zero-shot methods, despite using a single datasets collected with a single camera system.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To summarize, we present the following contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">a novel canonical transformation that enables the exploitation of vertical image position cue across diverse perspective geometries, enhancing both training scalabilty and zero-shot generalization,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">a model architecture for the probabilistic fusion of depth maps estimated using object size and vertical image position cues,</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">a thorough ablation of different depth cues, with insights previously unseen in the literature.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Domain-dependent Monocular Depth Estimation.</span> In a seminal work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, learning-based MDE has been established as a supervised dense regression task via ground-truth data obtained by reprojection of LiDAR scans.
Subsequent works improve upon the original approach by introducing various architectural novelties, such as convolutional models with skip connections between encoder and decoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, integration of conditional random fields <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>, adversarial training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> or attention-based architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
Unfortunately, these methods are specifically fine-tuned for accuracy on well established indoor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> and outdoor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> benchmarks, <em id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">experiencing significant accuracy degradation under distribution shifts</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Domain-agnostic Monocular Depth Estimation.</span> The inherent ambiguity and interdependence between camera parameters and depth present challenges for training a robust MDE model that generalizes across a wide range of environments.
As datasets are usually collected with a single camera system, models tend to act discriminatively and associate perspective geometry parameters with the pertaining environment.
Relative depth estimation methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> bypass camera parameter dependency by estimating depth with an unknown scale.
While these approaches achieve visually impressive results, <em id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">their inability to estimate metric depth limits their applicability</em>, often necessitating integration with additional sensors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">ZoeDepth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> is the first work to show satisfactory metric accuracy across different domains by fine-tuning a pre-trained relative depth estimation model on a single dataset with metric scale.
ZeroDepth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> chooses a different approach by providing the model with embedding of camera parameters, effectively disambiguating the features from the specifics of the camera system.
Metric3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> addresses the focal length-depth ambiguity by estimating depth in a canonical space defined through focal length denormalization.
UniDepth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> introduces a universal approach, simultaneously predicting both the depth and camera parameters, enabling metric depth estimation for images acquired with unknown sensors.
Although these methods demonstrate impressive results, <em id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">they rely on abundance of training data and computational resources</em>.
Furthermore, they are not truly zero-shot, as they tend to overfit to the typically high training resolution, hindering real-time performance on resource-constrained devices that require low-resolution estimation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Planar Constraints for Depth Estimation.</span> Real-world scenes are often highly regular, featuring numerous planar structures that can serve as additional cues to guide depth estimation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>.
A highly relevant application of MDE is in autonomous driving and mobile robotics, where a fixed relation between the camera system and the ground plane induces additional perspective geometry constraints.
It has been shown that models heavily utilize the corresponding ground-contact cues, completely disregarding the object size cue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
Moreover, incorporating ground plane constraint within the model enhances overall model accuracy, both in supervised <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>, and self-supervised training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>. However, these methods leverage the known perspective geometry constraints to enhance depth estimation only for road pixels, leading to limited generalization capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Proposed Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Preliminaries.</span> In this work, we examine an extremely common application domain of MDE: ground vehicles or a robot with a fixed camera configuration.
Assuming an ego coordinate system <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{F}}_{\mathcal{E}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓕</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{F}}_{\mathcal{E}}</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(x\rightarrow,y{\scriptstyle\nearrow},z\odot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0em">↗</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0em">⊙</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x\rightarrow,y{\scriptstyle\nearrow},z\odot)</annotation></semantics></math> defined at the ground level, and camera coordinate system <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{F}}_{\mathcal{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓕</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{F}}_{\mathcal{C}}</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(x\rightarrow,y{\;\otimes},z{\scriptstyle\nearrow})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0em" encoding="application/x-tex">(x\rightarrow,y{\;\otimes},z{\scriptstyle\nearrow})</annotation></semantics></math>, we consider a camera system parameterized by intrinsic matrix <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐊</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{K}</annotation></semantics></math> and extrinsic matrix encoding="application/x-tex">{}^{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{E}}[\mathbf{R|t}]</annotation></semantics></math>, where:</p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">and <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{t}=[0,0,-h]^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐭</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{t}=[0,0,-h]^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>,
with <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta,h)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta,h)</annotation></semantics></math> representing camera pitch and height, respectively.
Transformation of points from ego to camera coordinate frame is then: <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{C}}=\prescript{\mathcal{C}}{\mathcal{E}}{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{E}}+\mathbf{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>𝐑𝐩</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mrow></mrow><mprescripts></mprescripts><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></mmultiscripts><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐭</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{C}}=\prescript{\mathcal{C}}{\mathcal{E}}{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{E}}+\mathbf{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We disregard the camera yaw and roll in our parameterization; yaw has no effect on our canonical transformations, while roll is typically negligible in real-world setups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Problem Statement.</span>
We aim to learn a dense mapping <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:(\mathbf{I},\bm{\mathcal{C}})\mapsto\mathbf{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi>𝐃</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:(\mathbf{I},\bm{\mathcal{C}})\mapsto\mathbf{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3},\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3},\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W}</annotation></semantics></math> being RGB image and a correspondending depth map, and <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}</annotation></semantics></math> representing camera parameterization in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3 Proposed Method ‣ GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Most importantly, the learned mapping should be able to generalize to images acquired with arbitrary camera system.
In contrast to existing zero-shot methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, which rely on multiple datasets with varying camera parameters, we aim to learn this mapping using data acquired with a single camera system <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{Train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mtext>Train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{Train}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Depth Cues</h3>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2412.06080v2/car.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/202;" width="685" height="202"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Depth cues in MDE for ground vehicles<span id="S3.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Depth <math id="S3.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> can be calculated both as a function of imaging size <math id="S3.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> (with corresponding known object size <math id="S3.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>) and as a function of vertical image position <math id="S3.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Monocular depth estimation relies on semantic and geometric cues in the training data to solve the depth ambiguity of monocular perspective geometry.
As illustrated in <a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3.1 Depth Cues ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, one of the possible cues to regress depth <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is the relation between object’s real-world size <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and imaging size <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=f_{y}\frac{S}{s}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=f_{y}\frac{S}{s}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">However, this cue leads to entanglement between focal length and depth, leading to generalization issues when camera parameters change.
Recent zero-shot methods address this issue by embedding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, estimating <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> or disentangling the focal length <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.
A major drawback of this cue is its reliance on the object’s real world size <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, which is highly dependent on the particular environmental domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For ground vehicles, a fixed position of the camera system relative to the ground introduces an additional perspective geometry constraint – known depth of the ground plane, which is constant for all images acquired by the same camera setup.
For each pixel <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math>, depth <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is calculated from the intersection of the camera rays <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\,\mathbf{K}^{-1}[u,v,1]^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐊</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\,\mathbf{K}^{-1}[u,v,1]^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> and the ground plane <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(^{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{E}}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{n}_{\mathcal{E}})^{T}\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{C}}+h=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>𝐑𝐧</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(^{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{E}}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{n}_{\mathcal{E}})^{T}\mathbf{p}_{\mathcal{C}}+h=0</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{n}_{\mathcal{E}}=[0,0,1]^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐧</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{n}_{\mathcal{E}}=[0,0,1]^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> being the upward ground normal.
This constraint enables depth regression via object’s ground contact point:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle d</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{-h}{(^{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{E}}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{n}_{\mathcal{E}})^{T}\mathbf{K}^{-1}[u,v,1]^{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></msub><mi>𝐑𝐧</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>𝐊</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{-h}{(^{\mathcal{C}}_{\mathcal{E}}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{n}_{\mathcal{E}})^{T}\mathbf{K}^{-1}[u,v,1]^{T}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E3Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{f_{y}h}{\left(H-c_{y}-y\right)\cos(\theta)-f_{y}\sin(\theta)}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{f_{y}h}{\left(H-c_{y}-y\right)\cos(\theta)-f_{y}\sin(\theta)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=H-v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=H-v</annotation></semantics></math> represents vertical image position of the ground projection, as visualized in <a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3.1 Depth Cues ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Compared to the object size cue, which is entirely semantic, this cue implicitly encodes the known perspective geometry constraints of the scene, thereby inducing a valuable prior to the ill-posed MDE problem.
<em id="S3.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">However, it is highly reliant on accurate and consistent camera calibration.</em></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Canonical Transforms</h3>

<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2412.06080v2/system.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:617/277;" width="617" height="277" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Model architecture<span id="S3.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Given the input image and corresponding camera parameters, our model predicts two canonical depth representations, <math id="S3.F3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{C_{F}},\mathbf{C_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{C_{F}},\mathbf{C_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math> and corresponding uncertanties <math id="S3.F3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}},\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}},\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math>. Canonical representations are disentangled from the corresponding camera parameters, enabling separate exploitation of object size cue and vertical image position cue. Canonical representations are then transformed into depth maps <math id="S3.F3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{D_{F}},\mathbf{D_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{D_{F}},\mathbf{D_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which are subsequently adaptively fused into a final depth map <math id="S3.F3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐃</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}</annotation></semantics></math> based on estimated uncertanties.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Metric3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> proposed a canonical transform disentangling the predicted depth and camera parameters, enabling the use of object size cue for arbitrary camera systems.
To achieve this, depth is predicted in canonical space <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C_{F}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C_{F}}</annotation></semantics></math> with a canonical focal length <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, and post-processed to metric depth <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D_{F}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D_{F}}</annotation></semantics></math> by applying Focal Canonical Transform <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{FCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>FCT</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{FCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D_{F}}=\mathrm{FCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\mathbf{C_{F}})=\frac{f_{y}}{f_{c}}\mathbf{C_{F}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>FCT</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D_{F}}=\mathrm{FCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\mathbf{C_{F}})=\frac{f_{y}}{f_{c}}\mathbf{C_{F}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}=\{f_{y}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}=\{f_{y}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Besides the object size cue, in this paper we propose to leverage the vertical image position cue, effectively encoding the configuration of the scene’s perspective geometry.
Unfortunately, this cue also induces entanglement between camera parameters and depth.
To enhance cross-dataset generalization, we introduce an additional canonical transform, which enables consistent exploitation of the ground plane prior.
Under this formulation, the model estimates a dense map <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C_{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C_{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math> representing vertical image position of the ground projection point.
Metric depth <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D_{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D_{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math> is then obtained via Vertical Canonical Transform <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{VCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>VCT</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{VCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{VCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\mathbf{C_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>VCT</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{VCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\mathbf{C_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to mapping <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\mapsto d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\mapsto d</annotation></semantics></math> obtainable from <a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.1 Depth Cues ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
Therefore, this transformation requires knowledge of camera parameters <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}=\{f_{y},c_{y},h,\theta\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}=\{f_{y},c_{y},h,\theta\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Crucially, <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">the proposed canonical space remains consistent under variations of camera parameters, facilitating generalization to diverse scenarios.</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The proposed <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{VCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>VCT</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{VCT}_{\bm{\mathcal{C}}}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is related to the depth of the ground plane, frequently used to enhance MDE accuracy in autonomous driving scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>.
However, these methods exploit the ground-plane constraint exclusively for road pixels, resulting in limited generalization capability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Model Architecture</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both cues have their advantages and drawbacks. For example, vertical position cue is highly consistent across environments due to the reduced reliance on semantic information.
However, it is highly sensitive to calibration errors, and performs worse as depth increases. An ideal model should leverage both cues, taking into account the confidence for respective image regions.
To that end, as visualized in <a href="#S3.F3" title="In 3.2 Canonical Transforms ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ GVDepth: Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Estimation for Ground Vehicles based on Probabilistic Cue Fusion" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we design our model to predict depth maps with both cues separately, and then fuse them into a final depth map based on the estimated aleatoric uncertainty.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use a standard encoder-decoder model with skip connections to process and upsample image features, gaining <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times C}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(h,w)=(\frac{H}{2},\frac{W}{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(h,w)=(\frac{H}{2},\frac{W}{2})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We forward these features to two very small UNet networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, producing our canonical representations <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{C_{F}},\mathbf{C_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐂</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{C_{F}},\mathbf{C_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math> and accompanying uncertainty estimates <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}},\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}},\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Canonical representations are forwarded to <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FCT}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>FCT</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FCT}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{VCT}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>VCT</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{VCT}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, obtaining <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{D_{F}},\mathbf{D_{Y}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{D_{F}},\mathbf{D_{Y}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which are then fused into a final depth map <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}=\frac{\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}\odot\mathbf{D_{F}}+\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}}\odot\mathbf{D_{Y}}}{\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}+\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}=\frac{\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}\odot\mathbf{D_{F}}+\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}}\odot\mathbf{D_{Y}}}{\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}+\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Geometric Augmentation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Contrary to zero-shot methods trained on multiple datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, we aim to achieve similar generalization capabilities by training on a single camera system.
However, without geometric diversity induced by varying camera parameters, model can simply disregard our proposed canonical transformations.
Therefore, we apply geometric augmentations, namely random cropping and resizing, to simulate different camera perspectives.
Crucially, compared to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, we train our model with multiple resolutions, enabling generalization for arbitrary image sizes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Optimization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our main training objective is to guide the fused depth map <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐃</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}</annotation></semantics></math> towards the ground-truth depth <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Given the distance in the <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{log}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>log</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{log}</annotation></semantics></math> domain <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{E}=\log(\mathbf{D})-\log(\mathbf{D}^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐄</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐃</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{E}=\log(\mathbf{D})-\log(\mathbf{D}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math>, the <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{SI}_{\mathrm{log}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>SI</mi><mi>log</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{SI}_{\mathrm{log}}</annotation></semantics></math> loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> is defined as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SI}_{\log}}=\alpha\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[\mathbf{E}]+\lambda\mathbb{E}^{2}[\mathbf{E}]}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>SI</mi><mi>log</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mi>𝕍</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝔼</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SI}_{\log}}=\alpha\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[\mathbf{E}]+\lambda\mathbb{E}^{2}[\mathbf{E}]},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=10</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0.15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0.15</annotation></semantics></math> as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, and <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝕍</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{V}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝔼</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}</annotation></semantics></math> being variance and expectation, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we enhance depth estimation accuracy from both canonical transformations by employing an uncertainty-weighted loss:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{unc}}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>unc</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{unc}}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\,\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}}^{-1}\odot||\mathbf{D_{F}-D^{*}}||_{1}+\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}^{-1}\odot||\mathbf{D_{Y}-D^{*}}||_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐘</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\,\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}}^{-1}\odot||\mathbf{D_{F}-D^{*}}||_{1}+\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}^{-1}\odot||\mathbf{D_{Y}-D^{*}}||_{1}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+\log(\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}})+\log(\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">+</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐅</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>𝐘</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+\log(\mathbf{\Sigma_{F}})+\log(\mathbf{\Sigma_{Y}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.2" class="ltx_p">which is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood, but with L1 norm instead of L2.
This approach down-weights regions where each cue exhibits higher uncertainty, encouraging each cue to focus on specific parts of the image where it performs better.
To facilitate training stability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, we predict <math id="S3.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> uncertainties, and perform <math id="S3.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\exp(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\exp(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> operation accordingly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, same as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, we employ geometric consistency loss. Given two different sets of geometric augmentations of the same image (<math id="S3.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>), geometric consistency loss is defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}}=\left\|\mathcal{T}_{2}\circ\mathcal{T}_{1}^{-1}\circ\mathbf{D}_{1}-\operatorname{sg}\left(\mathbf{D}_{2}\right)\right\|_{1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>con</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>sg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}}=\left\|\mathcal{T}_{2}\circ\mathcal{T}_{1}^{-1}\circ\mathbf{D}_{1}-\operatorname{sg}\left(\mathbf{D}_{2}\right)\right\|_{1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are estimated depth maps for i’th augmentation, and <math id="S3.SS5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{sg}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>sg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{sg}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the stop-gradient operation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our final loss is a linear combination:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SI}_{\log}}+\lambda_{\text{unc}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{unc}}+\lambda_{\text{con}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>SI</mi><mi>log</mi></msub></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>unc</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>unc</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>con</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>con</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SI}_{\log}}+\lambda_{\text{unc}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{unc}}+\lambda_{\text{con}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p5.2" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S3.SS5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{unc}}=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>unc</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{unc}}=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{con}}=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>con</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{con}}=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets.</span>
We use a diverse set of autonomous driving datasets, each collected with a different camera setup.
Specifically, we utilize an aggregation of KITTI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, DDAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, DrivingStereo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, Waymo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> and Argoverse Stereo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> datasets.
Due to the missing and sometimes inaccurate information, we calibrate extrinsic parameters, i.e., camera height and pitch, which are required for our canonical representation.
Further details are provided in the supplementary materials.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation Details.</span>
We use a standard encoder-decoder with skip connections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
In all experiments we use a ConvNext-Large <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> encoder initialized with ImageNet weights.
To provide the model with additional contextual information, we fuse ground plane embedding in the decoder layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>.
In our depth cue fusion model, secondary U-Nets are designed with a lightweight structure, containing only three convolutional layers for both downsampling and upsampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our models are trained in PyTorch <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> with an AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>.
Learning rate is progressively reduced with Cosine Annealing from 1e-4 to 1e-5.
For all datasets, we use random cropping and resizing to <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in[200,500]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>200,500</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in[200,500]</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> chosen to preserve the aspect ratio after cropping.
To increase resolution diversity in a single batch update, we perform gradient accumulation for 2 training steps.
All models are trained for 150000 optimizer steps with an effective batch size of 16, on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.
Compared to concurrent zero-shot methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, this constitutes a fairly simple training setup, both in computational and data resources, demonstrating the efficiency of our approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Details.</span>
We use established depth metrics: absolute relative error (<math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{A.Rel}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi>Rel</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{A.Rel}</annotation></semantics></math>), root mean squared error (<math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{RMS}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>RMS</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{RMS}</annotation></semantics></math>), root mean squared log error (<math id="S4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{RMS}_{\log})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><msub><mi>RMS</mi><mi>log</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{RMS}_{\log})</annotation></semantics></math> and accuracy <math id="S4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{\delta}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{\delta}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> under a threshold <math id="S4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.25^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>1.25</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.25^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. Depth is evaluated in the metric range of [0 m, 80 m].</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate GVDepth at an image resolution of <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\times 640" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>640</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\times 640</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> varies according to the dataset to preserve the original aspect ratio. For a fair comparison, domain-specific models are trained and tested using the same image dimensions, which depend on specific dataset.
All models are evaluated using a ConvNext-L backbone if available; otherwise, we select the backbone with the most similar complexity.
For zero-shot methods, we use the provided checkpoints.
For metric zero-shot models which are optimized for a specific training resolution, we report results at both their original training resolution and our testing resolution for a comprehensive evaluation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Evaluation of Zero-shot Accuracy</h3>

<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Generalization capability comparison.<span id="S4.T1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Domain-dependent methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> are trained and evaluated on our evaluation setup at an <math id="S4.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\times 640" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>640</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\times 640</annotation></semantics></math> resolution. Zero-shot methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> are evaluated with provided checkpoints. (†): Shift and scale alignment with ground-truth. (‡): Resizing and padding to native training resolution.
